tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

schema.name: ToolSearch
schema.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-REDACTED> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

content.content:
# The RFQ Inbox — a four-day problem

> Read *The situation*, then open the twenty-four dev emails, then come back for the rest. This
> document is short on purpose: most of what matters here is *your* judgment, not ours.

## The situation

You have just joined **Ridgeline Industrial Supply**, a distributor of pipe, fittings, flanges,
valves and bolting. Ridgeline's inside sales reps spend most of their day on one inbox:
customers asking for prices. On a good day that is a tidy list in the body of an email. Most
days it's a spreadsheet with "ALL PIPE SCH 40" in a merged cell above the rows that need it, a
phone photo of a list a foreman wrote on a clipboard, a scan of a scan, a reply that says
"make #3 twelve and kill #5" to an email from last week, a supplier's quote that looks exactly
like a customer's request, and a bounce notification with somebody's whole order attached.

Every one of those has to become a clean list of what the customer wants — or a flag saying a
human needs to look — before anyone can quote it. A missed email is a customer who never
hears back. A line read wrong is a wrong quote.

**Your job: build the thing that reads this inbox.** For every email, decide what kind of email
it is, and pull out exactly the items being asked for, each one self-contained — with the
schedule, material or rating that the customer wrote somewhere *other* than on that line.

You will need a model to do it — several of these emails are photos and scans, and most of
the rest hide their meaning in headings, notes and threads. Calling a model is the easy part.
What we are assessing is **how you put it to work**: what it decides and what your code checks,
how you know it's right, what it costs, and what happens when it's wrong, slow, or down.

## What you are given

```
data/
  README.md            the contract: the command, the output format, how we grade — read it in full
  eml_to_json.py       optional helper: .eml → JSON + the attachment files
  check_format.py      validates your output's shape (it scores nothing)
  catalog.csv          what Ridgeline stocks — for the optional matcher
  dev/
    emails/*.eml       24 inbox emails
    answer_key.json    what a careful rep made of each one — your ground truth
```

There is also a **held-out inbox** of ~40 emails from the same company — the same kinds of
customers, documents and surprises, none of the same strings, and a few situations dev doesn't
show you. We run your submission against it. Work that passes dev by fitting it will not
survive that; work built from understanding *why* dev is hard will. All data is synthetic.

## What to build

One command, exactly as `data/README.md` defines it:

```
parse --emails <dir> --out parsed.json
```

Per email: a **classification** (seven kinds), the **line items** (verbatim text,
self-contained description, quantity, unit, where it came from), and a **needs-review** flag
for when you can't — or shouldn't — answer alone.

**Build it like it will run on the real inbox tomorrow.** Four properties are required, and we
test each of them:

1. **Replayable.** On the dev inbox it runs with **no API key** — record or cache model
   responses and commit them.
2. **Idempotent and cheap to re-run.** Running it twice on the same inbox makes no new model
   calls the second time.
3. **One bad email never takes down the run.** Some attachments are broken on purpose; some
   things are unreadable for anyone. Those come back flagged, and the run carries on.
4. **You know what it cost.** Tell us the model calls, tokens and dollars per email on dev.

## Optional — if you have time left

Never required, never penalised when skipped. If you build the matcher we run its numbers too,
but both parts are weighed in the interview, not in your score. Both are good places to show
judgment the core can't.

- **The matcher, designed (and built if you like).** Each extracted line eventually has to
  become a catalog part — or a decision that Ridgeline doesn't stock it. The catalog does not
  carry everything customers ask for, and the closest part is often one attribute off (right
  size, wrong schedule). Write down how you'd decide: what you normalise, which attributes
  must agree, how you find candidates, when the answer is **not in catalog** and when it is
  "ask the customer", where a model helps and what it must never decide on its own, and how
  you'd measure it. A page in `DECISIONS.md` or a separate `MATCHER.md`. If you build it, add
  the optional `sku` / `match` fields `data/README.md` defines — `dev/answer_key.json` has
  the answers for dev.
- **A small web app** that walks one email through your system: the email and its
  attachments, the lines you extracted and where each came from, and — if you built the
  matcher — each line's catalog match or not-in-catalog decision, which a rep can accept or
  overturn. Clarity is worth something; polish is worth nothing.

## What to hand in

A git repository — zipped, on Google Drive, or on GitHub (see *Logistics*) — containing:

1. **The code**, with `RUNNING.md`: one setup step from a fresh clone or unzip to a working
   `parse`, the model(s) you use, and what a run costs.
2. **`parsed.json` for dev**, regenerated by your command.
3. **`DECISIONS.md`** — at most two pages. These four headed sections are **required**:
   - *Something in the data that surprised you* — one paragraph.
   - *Something in this brief or the README you disagree with, and what you did about it.*
     We mean it; the README is not gospel.
   - *Your predicted held-out numbers, and the two kinds of email you expect to get wrong.*
     We will compare.
   - *How this runs for real.* Three thousand emails a day arrive by webhook. The model
     provider is down for two hours. A customer sends a 300-page PDF. The same email is
     delivered twice. What happens in your design — and which of those did you actually
     build?

   Plus whatever else belongs in a design memo: where the model decides and where code
   decides, how you measured it, what you rejected, what you know is broken, what's next.
   Be specific to *this* data.
4. **`AI_USAGE.md`** — at most one page, how you used AI coding agents (Claude Code, Codex,
   Cursor, Copilot — whatever you use for real work), with these headings:
   - *Setup* — which tools and models; instruction files, subagents, skills, MCP servers.
   - *How you worked* — one paragraph: how you split the work, planned, tested and reviewed.
   - *Three moments* — the agent was wrong and how you caught it; you overruled it and why;
     it saved you real time. Each points at a commit hash **and** the session it happened in.
5. **`ai-sessions/`** — the raw session logs of your coding agents for this project, unedited
   except for redacted secrets: Claude Code — the `.jsonl` files under
   `~/.claude/projects/<your-project-folder>/` (or `/export` from each session); Codex CLI —
   `~/.codex/sessions/`; Cursor, Copilot and others — export or copy each chat. Include every
   instruction you gave the agents (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, rules files, subagent or skill
   definitions, saved prompts). We read **how you directed the tools** — what you asked for,
   what you checked, what you threw away — not how much of the code you typed. If your tool
   can't export, say so in `AI_USAGE.md` and bring the history to the interview. **Before you
   send:** search the folder for `sk-` and redact any key (agents often echo `.env` files into
   tool output), and include only this project's instruction files — nothing personal or
   belonging to an employer.
6. **A screen recording, five minutes or less** — one email end to end through your system,
   the two decisions you'd defend first, and one moment from your agent sessions where you
   changed the agent's course. Production value is worth nothing. Link it in
   `RUNNING.md` or commit it (keep the repo under 50 MB).
7. **Commit history as it happened** — a zip must include the `.git` folder; a GitHub repo
   carries it already. Don't squash or tidy it for us.

## Rules

- **Time.** The package arrives **Thursday 12 November**; submission is due **Sunday
  15 November, 23:59 CST** — and the moment you're done is the moment to send it. We expect **8–12 hours of work** and grade for that budget. Past 16
  hours: stop and write. Tell us in `DECISIONS.md` roughly how long you spent. If this window
  doesn't work for you, say so and we'll move it.
- **Stack.** Anything that runs for us: we run submissions on **Windows — natively, in Docker,
  or under WSL** — with Python 3.11+, Node 20 and Docker available. If your stack assumes
  Linux, ship a Dockerfile; either way, say what we need in `RUNNING.md`.
- **Model access.** The email this package came with includes an **OpenAI API key with a USD
  20 cap**. It is for your `parse` command — run your coding agents on your own accounts. Read
  it from `OPENAI_API_KEY` and name the model(s) in `RUNNING.md`. We run the held-out inbox
  **with an OpenAI key only**, so your default path must use OpenAI; another provider is
  welcome as an option you switch on, at your own cost. If the key is missing or a call fails,
  your system degrades the way you designed it to — it never crashes.
- **Don't fit the dev set.** The held-out inbox has the same *kinds* of surprises, not the same
  strings.
- **No outbound side effects.** Nothing in your submission sends email or calls anything except
  the model provider.

## How we read it

We run `parse` on the held-out inbox **before we read a word you wrote** — once with our key,
then again with the key removed (property 2 says that second run should match, from your
cache). Then `DECISIONS.md`, the recording, the code, the commits, `AI_USAGE.md` and your
agent sessions. Then a 60-minute conversation: you show us the two emails you find most
interesting, predict what your system will do with an email you've never seen before we run
it, defend two decisions, and change something live — with whatever tools you normally use.
We watch where you look first and what test you name.

Two pages that name three real properties of this data beat a feature you rushed.

## Logistics

- **Submit:** reply to the email this package came with, carrying **one** of: a GitHub
  repository link (if it's private, ask in your reply and we'll tell you who to add); a Google
  Drive link to the zip (project folder including `.git`, fixtures committed); or the zip
  attached — but mail servers often reject zips containing scripts and cap attachments around
  25 MB, so prefer a link. Code and recording both.
- **Your code stays yours.** We use it only to evaluate you and delete it when the process ends.
- **Questions:** reply on the same email thread. We answer **08:00–17:00 CST every day,
  weekend included**, usually within a few hours. We answer questions about the data and the
  format; we won't tell you what to build.=====
# data/ — the files, the contract, the grading

```
dev/emails/*.eml       the inbox: 24 RFC-822 emails (E001.eml …) — plain text, HTML, Excel,
                       CSV, Word, text PDFs, scanned PDFs, phone photos, pasted screenshots, threads
dev/answer_key.json    what a careful inside sales rep (ISR) made of each email — your ground truth
check_format.py        validates the shape of your output (it scores nothing)
catalog.csv            what Ridgeline stocks — used only by the OPTIONAL matcher (see the end)
eml_to_json.py         optional: .eml → JSON + the attachment files. Use it, port it, or ignore it —
                       unpacking MIME is not what we grade; reading what is inside the attachments is.
```

A **held-out inbox** from the same company — same kinds of customers, documents and surprises,
none of the same strings — is not shipped; your submission is run against it.

## The command (this is how we run you, so the shape is mandatory)

```
<your command> parse --emails <dir> --out parsed.json
```

It reads every `.eml` in `<dir>` and writes one JSON file. Check it with
`python check_format.py parsed.json --emails <dir>` (exit 0 = shape ok).

## parsed.json

One object keyed by the `.eml` filename stem. **Every email in the directory must appear.**

```json
{
  "E003": {
    "classification": "rfq",
    "revises": null,
    "duplicate_of": null,
    "needs_review": false,
    "review_reason": null,
    "line_items": [
      {
        "raw": "2\" x 21' - 12 lengths",
        "description": "2\" pipe, SCH 40 A53B ERW, threaded & coupled, 21' lengths",
        "qty": 12,
        "uom": "EA",
        "source": "body"
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

### classification — exactly one per email

| value | the **current** message … | line_items |
|---|---|---|
| `rfq` | asks us to price or check availability of items | the items |
| `rfq_revision` | changes a request made earlier in the same thread (quantities, additions, removals) | the **complete** order as now intended; `revises` = the earlier email's id if it is in the inbox, else null |
| `purchase_order` | commits to buy — a PO, "please process", "go ahead with items 1–3" | the items ordered |
| `vendor_quote` | is a supplier quoting or answering **us** | `[]` |
| `status_inquiry` | asks about an existing quote or order (update? ETA? tracking?) | `[]` |
| `auto_reply` | is machine-generated: out-of-office, bounce, receipt | `[]` |
| `other` | anything else: marketing, invoices and remittances, job applications, internal chatter, "we went with someone else" | `[]` |

Classify what the current message *does* — not the subject line, not the quoted history.

### line_items — one per thing the customer is asking for

- **What counts.** Items in the current message, its attachments and pasted pictures, and —
  when one of our own reps forwards a customer's email — in the forwarded content. Not items
  in quoted earlier messages (they were handled when they arrived), not headings, notes,
  totals, prices, signatures, crossed-out lines, or old revisions of a document.
- **`raw`** — the line's text as it appears where you found it (a table row's cells on one
  line; for a picture or scan, your reading of it). We pair your lines with ours on these
  tokens, so keep it close to the source.
- **`description`** — the item **self-contained**, as an ISR would type it into a quote
  without re-reading the email: the line's own words plus every heading, note, column
  header, sheet name, form field, subject line or earlier line that applies to it — and
  nothing that doesn't apply to it. Never invent a spec the email doesn't give.
- **`qty` / `uom`** — as the customer stated it, not converted. A number spelled out is a
  number; a vague amount ("a couple", "enough for the job") is `null`. A size, schedule,
  length, rating, part number or price is never a quantity. `uom` is one of `EA FT M IN BX
  PK PR DZ RL LB SET GAL BAG CS`, or `null` when no unit is stated (we read `null` as `EA`).
- **`source`** — `"body"`, or the filename of the attachment / pasted image the line came from.

### Threads, duplicates, forwards

- A reply that changes an earlier request → `rfq_revision` with the **complete** order as the
  customer now intends it; the earlier email keeps its own lines as they were on arrival.
- The same request sent twice → **the email with the later `Date:` is the duplicate**: same
  classification as the original, `duplicate_of` = the original's id, `line_items: []`.
- Anything **from** `@ridgeline-supply.example` is one of our own reps, usually forwarding a
  customer's email; classify it as the customer's email, and read the rep's own note too.

### needs_review — "a human has to look at this before anyone quotes it"

`true` when the email asks for something you cannot fully read or resolve: the attachment it
points at is missing or can't be opened, or the items themselves are only identified by
something that isn't in the email ("same as our last order, but double it"). Put the reason in `review_reason` (required when `true`) and still
return whatever lines you *could* read. Only for `rfq`, `rfq_revision` and `purchase_order`.

## Optional: matching to the catalog

If you build the optional matcher, add three fields to each line item:

```json

# DECISIONS

**Time spent:** about __ hours. <!-- fill in -->

## Shape of the system — who decides what

`ingest` (code) → **one model call per email** (`gpt-5.4-mini-2026-03-17`, reasoning effort medium,
strict JSON schema) → `guards` (code) → `threads` (code).

- **Code reads the files.** Every part becomes text or images before the model sees it: xlsx with
  sheet state, merged cells, hidden rows and struck cells marked; docx in document order with
  tracked deletions removed; PDF rows rebuilt from word positions, scans rendered to images;
  HTML tables flattened with `~~strike~~` kept. A broken part becomes `kind=unreadable` with a
  note — it never raises.

  description (heading scope, overrides beating defaults, quoted history is not a request).

  model said; non-request classes carry no lines; a request with zero lines, an unreadable part
  or a truncated document is always `needs_review`; `source` must be a real part; `raw` is
  snapped to the unique matching source row (the model's copy of a row varies run to run, and
  graders pair on `raw`). If a numbered table row is accounted for by no line, the model is
  asked once more with that row named (caught a silently dropped PO line in E015, $0.004).

  `duplicate_of` needs the same sender, ≤30 days, identical attachment hashes and matching lines.

19-email stress inbox (`tests/stress/`) for situations dev doesn't show — tracked changes, a
Spanish request, a rotated photo, an invoice with item lines, "make #3 twelve and kill #5", a

system. Dev: 24/24 classes, 210/210 lines, 0 silent / 0 hallucinated, context 172/173.

`A53 Grade B`); a two-call classify-then-extract design — twice the cost, and the classifier
needs the same reading anyway.

## Something in the data that surprised you

The most request-shaped text in the inbox is usually not a request. E013's bounce carries a
perfect numbered list of valves with quantities — it is *our own* RFQ to a supplier. E011 is a
supplier's price list. E005's workbook is named `RevB` and hides a sheet `Rev A (old)` with the
superseded rows; a reader that loads every sheet quotes both revisions, and a model that sees the
filename calls it a revision although no earlier email exists. Meanwhile the real requests hide:
the spec is in a merged cell two rows above (`ALL FITTINGS BW SCH 40 A234 WPB UNLESS NOTED`) with
one row overriding it to SCH 80, or on a phone photo of a nameplate. So most of the accuracy came
from *ingest* — marking hidden, struck and merged structure faithfully — not from the prompt.

The README allows `needs_review` only on `rfq`, `rfq_revision` and `purchase_order`. But the
brief's own costliest failure is "a customer who never hears back", and some non-requests need a
person: a bounce of *our quote to a customer*, a "we went with someone else" that should close a
quote, an out-of-office from the buyer on a job with a deadline. Under the contract those come back

one-line reason for every classification; it is in `parsed.report.json` and the viewer, so a
person can see *why* something was set aside. In production I'd add a separate `attention`
field rather than overload `needs_review`. Not built.

guide. For ~40 held-out emails: **silent losses 0** (every request with no lines is flagged by
code), **hallucinated lines 2–5**, **lost/phantom 1–2**, classification **~90%**, line recall

1. **Photos and scans of handwritten lists.** The reading is all we have, so a misread `6`/`8`,

   cannot check a picture; only the review flag helps, and the model flags too rarely.
2. **Terse revisions against an earlier email that isn't in the inbox.** "Kill #5" needs the
   original list; when it's only partly quoted, the "complete order as now intended" will be
   incomplete or wrong. A second hazard on the same boundary: Rev B / resend / "also add" as new
   rfq vs revision — I chose "revision only if it changes an *earlier email*", which held-out
   may draw differently.

failures, a per-email header fallback, a 30-page cap, per-email isolation, and a per-email

  about **$22/day**. Median latency 4.9 s, worst 24 s; 3,000/day is ~2 per minute, so one worker
  keeps up. Design: the webhook stores the raw `.eml` and enqueues its hash; workers run
  `process_one`; thread linking moves from "whole inbox" to a lookup in a store of past emails by
  Message-ID, subject and domain.
- **Provider down for two hours.** Today: retries, then the breaker trips and every remaining
  email gets the fallback — headers decide auto_reply/bulk, everything else becomes
  `rfq` + `needs_review` ("not read automatically"). Fallbacks are not cached, so the next run
  calls the model for exactly those emails. For real I'd hold them in the queue with backoff
  for a while before handing them to people, with an alert — 250 emails to a person is worse
  than a 2-hour delay.

  "only the first 30 of 300 pages read" (stress S18). Next: split into page windows, one call each,
  merge lines, and still flag for review — a 300-page document is usually a spec book, not a list.

  cache key, so it costs nothing, and `threads` marks the later one `duplicate_of` the first
  (stress S13 is a byte copy). For real, dedupe on Message-ID + body hash at the webhook before
  any work.

- `raw` for pictures varies between runs (E023's nameplate); the cache makes it stable for
  replay, not right.
- Thread linking only sees the current inbox; there's no memory of last week.
- The optional matcher is not built.
- Next: page-window chunking, an `attention` field, and the matcher design (`size`/`spec`/
  `material`/`ends` must agree exactly; the model may propose, never decide).

# DECISIONS

**Time spent:** about __ hours. <!-- fill in -->

## Shape of the system — who decides what

`ingest` (code) → **one model call per email** (`gpt-5.4-mini-2026-03-17`, reasoning effort medium,
strict JSON schema) → `guards` (code) → `threads` (code).

- **Code reads the files.** Every part becomes text or images before the model sees it: xlsx with
  sheet state, merged cells, hidden rows and struck cells marked; docx in document order with
  tracked deletions removed; PDF rows rebuilt from word positions, scans rendered to images;
  HTML tables flattened with `~~strike~~` kept. A broken part becomes `kind=unreadable` with a
  note — it never raises.
- **The model judges.** Classification, which lines are requests, and the self-contained
  description (heading scope, overrides beating defaults, quoted history is not a request).
  The prompt states principles, not dev strings; its one worked example is invented.
- **Code checks anything that is a fact.** Struck and hidden-only lines are dropped whatever the
  model said; non-request classes carry no lines; a request with zero lines, an unreadable part
  or a truncated document is always `needs_review`; `source` must be a real part; `raw` is
  snapped to the unique matching source row (the model's copy of a row varies run to run, and
  graders pair on `raw`). If a numbered table row is accounted for by no line, the model is
  asked once more with that row named (caught a silently dropped PO line in E015, $0.004).
- **Code links threads.** `revises` from In-Reply-To/References, then subject + sender domain;
  `duplicate_of` needs the same sender, ≤30 days, identical attachment hashes and matching lines.

**Measured, not guessed.** I wrote a scorer that implements the README's grading, and a
19-email stress inbox (`tests/stress/`) for situations dev doesn't show — tracked changes, a
Spanish request, a rotated photo, an invoice with item lines, "make #3 twelve and kill #5", a
byte-identical second delivery, a 35-page PDF. Its answers were written **before** running the
system. Dev: 24/24 classes, 210/210 lines, 0 silent / 0 hallucinated, context 172/173.
Stress: 19/19 classes, 118/133 lines (the 15 missing are pages 31–35, flagged), 0 hallucinated.
**Rejected:** gpt-5.5 — 4.6× the cost and *worse* on context (it "corrected" `A53B` to
`A53 Grade B`); a two-call classify-then-extract design — twice the cost, and the classifier
needs the same reading anyway.

## Something in the data that surprised you

The most request-shaped text in the inbox is usually not a request. E013's bounce carries a
perfect numbered list of valves with quantities — it is *our own* RFQ to a supplier. E011 is a
supplier's price list. E005's workbook is named `RevB` and hides a sheet `Rev A (old)` with the
superseded rows; a reader that loads every sheet quotes both revisions, and a model that sees the
filename calls it a revision although no earlier email exists. Meanwhile the real requests hide:
the spec is in a merged cell two rows above (`ALL FITTINGS BW SCH 40 A234 WPB UNLESS NOTED`) with
one row overriding it to SCH 80, or on a phone photo of a nameplate. So most of the accuracy came
from *ingest* — marking hidden, struck and merged structure faithfully — not from the prompt.

## Something in the brief or README you disagree with

The README allows `needs_review` only on `rfq`, `rfq_revision` and `purchase_order`. But the
brief's own costliest failure is "a customer who never hears back", and some non-requests need a
person: a bounce of *our quote to a customer*, a "we went with someone else" that should close a
quote, an out-of-office from the buyer on a job with a deadline. Under the contract those come back
`auto_reply` / `other` with nothing to act on. **What I did:** kept the contract in
`parsed.json` (guards enforce it, because the grader scores it), and made the model state a
one-line reason for every classification; it is in `parsed.report.json` and the viewer, so a
person can see *why* something was set aside. In production I'd add a separate `attention`
field rather than overload `needs_review`. Not built.

## Predicted held-out numbers, and two kinds of email I expect to get wrong

Dev is 100% partly because I looked at it; the stress inbox (unseen until written) is the fairer
guide. For ~40 held-out emails: **silent losses 0** (every request with no lines is flagged by
code), **hallucinated lines 2–5**, **lost/phantom 1–2**, classification **~90%**, line recall
**~90%**, precision **~95%**, qty **~95%**, uom/source **~97%**, context carried **~85%**,
links mostly right, needs_review P/R **~80% / ~90%** (I flag on doubt).

1. **Photos and scans of handwritten lists.** The reading is all we have, so a misread `6`/`8`,
   a missed line or a `raw` that pairs badly with the key's reading costs qty and recall. Code
   cannot check a picture; only the review flag helps, and the model flags too rarely.
2. **Terse revisions against an earlier email that isn't in the inbox.** "Kill #5" needs the
   original list; when it's only partly quoted, the "complete order as now intended" will be
   incomplete or wrong. A second hazard on the same boundary: Rev B / resend / "also add" as new
   rfq vs revision — I chose "revision only if it changes an *earlier email*", which held-out
   may draw differently.

## How this runs for real

**Built today:** content-addressed cache (sha256 of model + effort + prompt + full content incl.
image bytes, atomic writes), 3 retries with timeout, a circuit breaker after 3 consecutive
failures, a per-email header fallback, a 30-page cap, per-email isolation, and a per-email
cost/token report. **Not built:** the webhook, a queue, a database.

- **3,000 emails a day.** Measured cost is $0.0072 per email (3,940 tokens incl. reasoning) →
  about **$22/day**. Median latency 4.9 s, worst 24 s; 3,000/day is ~2 per minute, so one worker
  keeps up. Design: the webhook stores the raw `.eml` and enqueues its hash; workers run
  `process_one`; thread linking moves from "whole inbox" to a lookup in a store of past emails by
  Message-ID, subject and domain.
- **Provider down for two hours.** Today: retries, then the breaker trips and every remaining
  email gets the fallback — headers decide auto_reply/bulk, everything else becomes
  `rfq` + `needs_review` ("not read automatically"). Fallbacks are not cached, so the next run
  calls the model for exactly those emails. For real I'd hold them in the queue with backoff
  for a while before handing them to people, with an alert — 250 emails to a person is worse
  than a 2-hour delay.
- **A 300-page PDF.** Today: the first 30 pages are read and the email is flagged
  "only the first 30 of 300 pages read" (stress S18). Next: split into page windows, one call each,
  merge lines, and still flag for review — a 300-page document is usually a spec book, not a list.
- **The same email delivered twice.** Built two ways: the second delivery hashes to the same
  cache key, so it costs nothing, and `threads` marks the later one `duplicate_of` the first
  (stress S13 is a byte copy). For real, dedupe on Message-ID + body hash at the webhook before
  any work.

## Known broken / next

- `raw` for pictures varies between runs (E023's nameplate); the cache makes it stable for
  replay, not right.
- Thread linking only sees the current inbox; there's no memory of last week.
- The optional matcher is not built.
- Next: page-window chunking, an `attention` field, and the matcher design (`size`/`spec`/
  `material`/`ends` must agree exactly; the model may propose, never decide).

"""python -m rfq parse --emails <dir> --out parsed.json"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import os
import sys
from pathlib import Path

from .config import ROOT, api_key
from .llm import LLM
from .pipeline import run

DEFAULT_MODEL = "gpt-5.4-mini-2026-03-17"
DEFAULT_EFFORT = "medium"  # bake-off on dev: low skimmed rules (ditto marks), gpt-5.5 cost 4.6x for no gain


def main(argv=None) -> int:
    sys.stdout.reconfigure(encoding="utf-8")
    sys.stderr.reconfigure(encoding="utf-8")
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="rfq")
    sub = ap.add_subparsers(dest="cmd", required=True)
    p = sub.add_parser("parse", help="parse every .eml in a directory")
    p.add_argument("--emails", type=Path, required=True)
    p.add_argument("--out", type=Path, required=True)
    p.add_argument("--model", default=os.environ.get("RFQ_MODEL", DEFAULT_MODEL))
    p.add_argument("--effort", default=os.environ.get("RFQ_EFFORT", DEFAULT_EFFORT), choices=["none", "minimal", "low", "medium", "high"])
    p.add_argument("--cache", type=Path, default=ROOT / "cache")
    p.add_argument("--workers", type=int, default=4)
    p.add_argument("--offline", action="store_true", help="never call the model; cache only")
    a = ap.parse_args(argv)

    if not a.emails.is_dir():
        print(f"--emails {a.emails} is not a directory", file=sys.stderr)
        return 2
    key = None if a.offline else api_key()
    if key is None:
        print("no OPENAI_API_KEY: replaying from cache; uncached emails will be flagged for review", file=sys.stderr)
    llm = LLM(a.model, a.effort, a.cache, key)
    rep = run(a.emails, a.out, llm, a.workers)
    t = rep["totals"]
    print(
        f"{t['emails']} emails -> {a.out} | model {rep['model']} ({rep['effort']}) | "
        f"new calls {t['model_calls']}, cache hits {t['cache_hits']}, fallbacks {t['fallbacks']} | "
        f"this run ${t['cost_usd_this_run']:.4f}, full inbox uncached ${t['cost_usd_if_uncached']:.4f} "
        f"(${t['avg_cost_usd_per_email']:.4f}/email, ~{t['avg_tokens_per_email']} tokens/email) | {t['wall_seconds']}s",
        file=sys.stderr,
    )
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

# RUNNING

Windows, native Python 3.11+ (developed and tested on 3.12.10). No Docker needed.

## Setup (one step, from a fresh clone or unzip)

```powershell
python -m venv .venv; .venv\Scripts\python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
```

(macOS/Linux/WSL: `python3 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt`)

## Run

```powershell
.venv\Scripts\python -m rfq parse --emails data\dev\emails --out parsed.json
```

- **With a key:** set `OPENAI_API_KEY` in the environment (or put `OPENAI_API_KEY=...` in a
  git-ignored `.env` in the repo root). New emails call the model; every answer is saved to
  `cache\`.
- **Without a key:** answers are replayed from `cache\`. On dev this reproduces the committed
  `parsed.json` byte for byte, with zero calls (checked from a fresh clone). An email with no
  cached answer is not dropped: it is classified from its headers and flagged `needs_review`.
- **A second run** on the same inbox makes no new model calls (the cache key is a sha256 of the
  model, effort, prompt and the email's full content).
- Every run also writes `parsed.report.json`: per-email calls, tokens, cost, cache hits,
  warnings and the model's one-line reason for its classification, plus totals.

Format check: `.venv\Scripts\python data\check_format.py parsed.json --emails data\dev\emails`
(24 emails, 0 problems).

## Model

`gpt-5.4-mini-2026-03-17` (a pinned snapshot, so a re-run can't drift), reasoning effort
`medium`, OpenAI Responses API with a strict JSON schema. One call per email, plus at most one
retry when code finds a numbered table row that no extracted line covers (1 of 24 dev emails).
Override with `--model` / `--effort` or `RFQ_MODEL` / `RFQ_EFFORT`. Other options: `--offline`
(never call the model), `--workers N` (default 4), `--cache DIR`.

## Cost (dev inbox, 24 emails, from `parsed.report.json`)

| | |
|---|---|
| model calls | 25 (24 + 1 coverage retry) |
| tokens per email | ~3,940 on average (input + output, incl. reasoning) |
| cost per email | **$0.0072** average |
| full inbox, uncached | **$0.17** |
| re-run / replay | $0.00 |
| latency per call | median 4.9 s, worst 24 s |

Prices used ($ per 1M tokens, `rfq/llm.py`): input 0.75, cached input 0.075, output 4.50.

## Other tools

```powershell
.venv\Scripts\python scripts\score.py parsed.json data\dev\answer_key.json      # score vs the key
.venv\Scripts\python -m rfq.viewer --emails data\dev\emails --parsed parsed.json --key data\dev\answer_key.json
                                                                   # local web view, one email end to end
.venv\Scripts\python -m pip install -r requirements-dev.txt; .venv\Scripts\python -m pytest -q   # 18 tests
.venv\Scripts\python -m rfq parse --emails tests\stress\emails --out tests\stress\parsed.json     # stress inbox
```

The viewer only reads local files and listens on `localhost:8765`.

"""Copy this project's Claude Code session logs into ai-sessions/, redacting secrets.

    python scripts/export_sessions.py [--src <~/.claude/projects/<folder>>]

Redacted: anything shaped like an OpenAI key (sk-...), the employer email domain, and the
Claude account email. Everything else is copied unedited. Re-run before submitting so the
folder holds the full, final sessions. Exits non-zero if anything key-shaped survives.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import re
import shutil
import sys
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
DEFAULT_SRC = Path.home() / ".claude" / "projects" / "c--Users-YashwanthYanala-Desktop-project"

RULES = [
    (re.compile(r"sk-[A-Za-z0-9_\-]{8,}"), "sk-REDACTED"),
    (re.compile(r"[A-Za-z0-9._%+\-]*@?[employer redacted](?:\.com)?", re.I), "[employer redacted]"),
    (re.compile(r"[A-Za-z0-9._%+\-]*[account email redacted][A-Za-z0-9._%+\-]*(?:@[A-Za-z0-9.\-]+)?", re.I), "[account email redacted]"),
]
KEYLIKE = re.compile(r"sk-(?!REDACTED)[A-Za-z0-9_\-]{8,}")


def redact(text: str) -> tuple[str, int]:
    n = 0
    for pat, rep in RULES:
        text, k = pat.subn(rep, text)
        n += k
    return text, n


def main() -> int:
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--src", type=Path, default=DEFAULT_SRC)
    ap.add_argument("--out", type=Path, default=ROOT / "ai-sessions")
    a = ap.parse_args()
    if a.out.exists():
        shutil.rmtree(a.out)
    total, files = 0, 0
    for f in sorted(a.src.rglob("*")):
        if not f.is_file():
            continue
        dest = a.out / f.relative_to(a.src)
        dest.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        text = f.read_bytes().decode("utf-8", errors="surrogateescape")
        text, n = redact(text)
        dest.write_bytes(text.encode("utf-8", errors="surrogateescape"))
        total, files = total + n, files + 1
    left = [p for p in a.out.rglob("*") if p.is_file() and KEYLIKE.search(p.read_text("utf-8", errors="replace"))]
    print(f"{files} files -> {a.out} | {total} redactions | key-shaped strings left: {len(left)}")
    return 1 if left else 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

# AI_USAGE

## Setup

- **Claude Code** in the VS Code extension, model **Claude Opus 5.5**, in one long session
  (`ai-sessions/92594963-78dc-4559-ba5d-13415136fa1e.jsonl`, continued across a context
  compaction).
- **No CLAUDE.md, custom subagents or saved prompts.** The only standing instruction is Claude
  Code's auto-memory file for this project (`ai-sessions/memory/`). It records the deadline, that I
  wanted the *why* explained at each step, and that the API key must never be printed.
- **Tools:** the agent's shell, file and web-search tools; Docker for a throwaway Python sandbox
  before Python was installed; the claude.ai Artifact tool for the hosted quote-desk page.
  No other MCP servers were used for this project.
- **The parser's own model** (OpenAI `gpt-5.4-mini`) ran on the assignment key. The agent never
  saw the key: it lives in a git-ignored `.env`.

## How you worked

I used the agent as a pair: it read the package, proposed the design, and explained each choice
before building it, and I made the calls: the git identity, keeping the key in `.env`, "model
extracts, code checks" with one call per email, and choosing the model by measurement
(I picked `gpt-5.4-mini` at medium after a three-way bake-off on cost against accuracy). Work went in small commits: ingest, then
the pipeline, then prompt versions. A scorer that implements the README's grading was written
early, and every change was judged by its numbers, not by eye. To avoid fitting dev, I asked for a
stress inbox of situations dev doesn't show, with its answers written *before* the system ran on
it. I reviewed results in a local viewer that shows one email end to end, and a hosted
quote-desk page that shows every extracted line.

## Three moments

1. **The agent was wrong, and a check caught it.** To stop Windows from rewriting the data
   files' line endings, the agent wrote a `.gitattributes` (`80f0d99`) in which the `*.json` /
   `*.md` text rules came *after* `data/**` and won, so the answer key and README would still
   have been converted. A byte-for-byte comparison of the committed data against the original
   package flagged the mismatches, and the rules were reordered (`22d7885`). This was verified
   at 0 mismatches. Lesson: "it's configured" is a claim; a byte check is evidence.
   Session `92594963`.
2. **I overruled it.** The agent's first commit used the git identity already configured on the
   machine, which was my work email. The brief says nothing belonging to an employer may go in,
   so I chose a personal identity. The agent set it repo-locally and re-authored the history
   (`7d55037` is the first commit under the personal identity). Session `92594963`.
3. **It saved real time.** The 19-email stress inbox, with its generator and expected answers
   (`85a86ef`), took minutes rather than an evening. It found two real bugs that dev scored as
   perfect: a repeat of a past order classified as a revision, and a purchase order whose second
   line was silently dropped. That led to the coverage check, which asks the model once more when
   a numbered row is missing. Session `92594963`.
